plants.region: Widely cultivated across Sub-Saharan Africa, originally from the sub-Himalayas
plants.primary_use: Nutritional supplement rich in vitamins A, C, and calcium; traditionally used for general weakness, anaemia and as a mild anti-inflammatory.
plants.preparation: Fresh or dried leaves are boiled into a tea (1 tablespoon dried leaves per cup of water, steep 5–10 min) or added to soups and porridge. Seeds are occasionally used for water purification.
plants.warnings: Root and root bark contain alkaloids and are NOT safe for pregnant women. Seeds in large quantities can cause diarrhoea. Do not replace prescribed medication without consulting a clinician.
plants.image_hints: Small ovate leaflets in opposite pairs on a feathery compound leaf; long pod-like seed capsules (drumsticks).

plants.region: Widely naturalised in East, West and Southern Africa
plants.primary_use: Traditionally used against malaria, skin infections, and as a mild antiseptic mouthwash.
plants.preparation: A decoction of fresh leaves (a handful boiled in 1 L water for 15 min) is taken in small cups. Twigs are chewed as a traditional toothbrush.
plants.warnings: Bitter and can be hepatotoxic in high doses. NOT safe for infants or pregnant women. Neem oil is strictly for external use.
plants.image_hints: Compound leaves with 8–19 serrated leaflets; small white fragrant flowers; yellow olive-like drupes.

plants.region: Widely cultivated across the continent; many closely-related endemic species (e.g. A. ferox, A. arborescens) are used similarly
plants.primary_use: Topical treatment of minor burns, skin irritation and insect bites; the inner gel is also used for mild constipation.
plants.preparation: Slit a mature leaf lengthwise and apply the clear inner gel directly to the skin. Avoid the yellow latex just beneath the skin — it is a strong purgative.
plants.warnings: The yellow latex (aloin) is a powerful laxative and is not safe during pregnancy or for people with kidney disease. Oral use for longer than a week is not recommended.
plants.image_hints: Thick fleshy green lance-shaped leaves with white serrations along the edges, growing in a rosette.

plants.region: Southern and Eastern Africa (highlands of South Africa, Lesotho, Ethiopia)
plants.primary_use: Traditionally used for colds, coughs, fevers and digestive complaints.
plants.preparation: A few fresh leaves are steeped in hot water for 5 minutes to make a bitter tea, or the leaves are inhaled as steam for blocked sinuses.
plants.warnings: Contains thujone. NOT safe during pregnancy, breastfeeding, or for people with seizure disorders. Use for no more than 3–5 days at a time.
plants.image_hints: Finely dissected grey-green aromatic leaves; small yellow flower heads; strong sage-like smell when crushed.

plants.region: Widely grown across West, Central and East Africa
plants.primary_use: Traditionally used as a mild diuretic and to support cardiovascular health; popular as a cooling drink (zobo / bissap / karkade).
plants.preparation: A handful of dried calyces is steeped in hot water with optional ginger and sugar to make a red tea.
plants.warnings: May lower blood pressure — use with caution if already on anti-hypertensive medication. NOT recommended in large amounts during pregnancy.
plants.image_hints: Deep red, fleshy, cup-shaped calyces around the seed pod; lobed green leaves with a reddish stem.

plants.primary_use: Nausea, indigestion, colds, and sore throat.
plants.preparation: Fresh rhizome is sliced and boiled in water (5–10 min) to make tea, often with lemon and honey.
plants.warnings: Large doses may increase bleeding risk — avoid before surgery or when on blood thinners. Generally safe in culinary amounts.
plants.image_hints: Knobbly, pale tan rhizome with fibrous interior; reed-like leafy stems growing from the rhizome.

plants.primary_use: Traditionally used as a general tonic for stress, fatigue, and loss of appetite.
plants.preparation: A teaspoon of dried leaves steeped in hot water for 5 minutes, taken up to three times a day.
plants.warnings: Bitter; NOT safe during pregnancy. Interactions with antiretrovirals are possible — people on HIV medication should consult a clinician first.
plants.image_hints: Silvery-grey pinnate leaves; bright red-orange pea-shaped flowers; inflated papery seed pods.

plants.region: Kalahari desert and surrounding savannahs (Namibia, Botswana, South Africa)
plants.primary_use: Traditionally used for arthritis, back pain, and digestive complaints.
plants.preparation: Dried tuber is simmered (1 teaspoon in 1 cup water for 10 min) to make a bitter tea. Also available as capsules.
plants.warnings: NOT safe for people with stomach ulcers or gallstones, and not during pregnancy. May interact with blood-thinners and diabetes medication.
plants.image_hints: Sprawling herb with lobed leaves; striking pinkish trumpet flowers; distinctive woody fruits covered in hooked claws.

plants.region: Highland forests of East, Central and Southern Africa
plants.primary_use: Traditionally used for urinary complaints and benign prostate hyperplasia (BPH).
plants.preparation: A small amount of dried bark is decocted in water for 10 minutes and taken as tea.
plants.warnings: The species is listed on CITES Appendix II — only harvest from sustainably managed sources. Overharvesting threatens wild populations. Consult a clinician for prostate issues.
plants.image_hints: Large evergreen tree with rough dark bark; lance-shaped leathery leaves with a serrated edge; small white flowers; purple-black cherry-like fruits.

plants.primary_use: Traditionally used for colds, chest complaints and fungal infections.
plants.preparation: A very small piece of bark is chewed for a peppery warmth in the chest, or leaves are steeped in hot water.
plants.warnings: Endangered species — the bark must be harvested only from cultivated trees or ethically managed reserves. Avoid during pregnancy.
plants.image_hints: Medium-sized tree; glossy leaves with a distinctive peppery taste when chewed.

plants.primary_use: Traditionally used for diabetes, fevers, intestinal parasites and as a digestive tonic.
plants.preparation: Leaves are washed and squeezed thoroughly in water to remove bitterness, then added to soups (bitter-leaf soup), or leaf juice is taken in small amounts.
plants.warnings: Excessive intake may lower blood sugar significantly — risky for people already on diabetes medication. Avoid in pregnancy due to possible uterine effects.
plants.image_hints: Soft-wooded shrub with elongated green leaves; very bitter taste; small clusters of off-white flower heads.

plants.region: Miombo woodlands of Southern and Central Africa (Zambia, Zimbabwe, Malawi, Mozambique)
plants.primary_use: Traditionally used for stomach pain, malaria, and STIs in parts of Zambia and Zimbabwe.
plants.preparation: Small pieces of root bark are boiled for 10–15 min and the decoction is taken in small cups.
plants.warnings: Strong and potentially toxic in excess — overdose has been linked to abortion and kidney strain. Do not self-medicate; consult a trained healer.
plants.image_hints: Small tree with bright yellow flowers and very long, slender, dark brown seed pods (up to 60 cm).

plants.primary_use: Fruit pulp is a rich source of vitamin C and used for diarrhoea and fevers; leaves are used as a vegetable and for respiratory complaints.
plants.preparation: Fruit pulp is dissolved in water or milk to make a tangy drink. Young leaves are boiled as a relish.
plants.warnings: Generally safe in food amounts. Bark and root preparations should only be used under supervision; over-harvesting damages the tree.
plants.image_hints: Massive swollen trunk; compound leaves with 5–7 leaflets arranged like fingers; large pendulous woody fruits.

plants.primary_use: Leaves used traditionally for fever and as a platelet-supportive remedy (e.g. in dengue-endemic areas); seeds for intestinal parasites.
plants.preparation: A few fresh leaves are blended with water and filtered; a small cup is taken once daily. Seeds can be chewed (up to 1 teaspoon per day).
plants.warnings: Unripe papaya and leaf preparations are NOT safe during pregnancy. Stop if any stomach pain occurs.
plants.image_hints: Palm-like unbranched trunk; large deeply-lobed leaves clustered at the top; oblong fruits with orange flesh and black seeds.

plants.primary_use: Fruit pulp is a mild laxative and cooling digestive; leaf decoctions are used for fevers.
plants.preparation: Pulp is soaked in warm water and the resulting sour liquid is drunk as a cooler or digestive.
plants.warnings: Generally safe in culinary amounts. Large laxative doses can cause cramping.
plants.image_hints: Large evergreen tree with feathery pinnate leaves; brown, brittle pods filled with sticky sour pulp and hard seeds.
